title: Building PRISM: a reflective AI product with an operational backend
summary: How streaming, concurrent generation cost control, cancellation cleanup, subscription consistency and privacy-conscious telemetry fit together in a bilingual iOS reflection app that is in internal QA.
lead: PRISM is a bilingual iOS self-reflection app with a Flutter client and an asynchronous Python backend. It is in internal QA and has not launched. This write-up focuses on the operational engineering: streaming generated text over server-sent events, reserving spend before a provider call, cleaning up interrupted requests, keeping subscriptions consistent, and keeping private text out of logs. It also states what has been verified and what has not.

sections.title: Context and product boundary
paragraphs: PRISM is a self-reflection product for iPhone. The experience centers on checking in, considering a question and returning to personal notes over time. The AI supports reflection; it is not positioned as prediction or therapy, and nothing here is a clinical claim.

That positioning shapes the engineering. A streamed response has to feel coherent, a saved entry has to stay private, and the interface has to work in both Vietnamese and English. The product is in internal QA and has not launched publicly, so this article describes design reasoning and implemented mechanisms, not production results.

The engineering problems below share a theme. Each is about a moment where the happy path stops being the whole story: a stream that is cut off, a spend that may or may not have happened, a purchase event that arrives late, a log line that could contain someone's private writing.

The stack is Flutter on the client, FastAPI with PostgreSQL and Redis on the backend, and RevenueCat for subscriptions. Each piece has a narrow role: PostgreSQL holds durable data, Redis holds the short-lived coordination state for generation, and RevenueCat is the source of subscription events. Keeping those roles separate is what lets the failure handling below stay understandable.

definitions.text: A one-way streaming channel from server to client over HTTP. Background: the server keeps the response open and sends text events as they are produced.
A hold placed before a provider call that represents expected spend. It is later settled against actual usage or released.
Whether an account currently has access to a paid capability, derived from durable subscription state.

sections.title: Connect a mobile app to a streaming service
paragraphs: I worked across a Flutter application and an asynchronous Python backend. The backend is the boundary between product behavior and the selected AI provider, so the provider can change without changing the client. Server-sent events deliver generated text incrementally.

Streaming adds states that a normal request and response does not have. A request is admitted, starts generating, streams partial text and may then be interrupted. The client has to tell a partial result from a completed one, and the server needs a defined cleanup path. Treating a disconnect as an ordinary success leaves both data and accounting inconsistent.

Keeping the provider behind the backend also keeps provider-specific details out of the app. The cost is that the backend owns more responsibility: it must translate whatever the provider returns into the stream the client expects, and it must decide what to do when that stream ends early.

One reason to choose server-sent events for this shape of problem is that the data flows in one direction, from the server to the app, while the request that starts it is an ordinary call. As background, SSE is simpler than a bidirectional channel because there is no need for the client to send messages on the same connection. The trade-off is that the client learns about a problem only through the stream itself, so the end of a stream needs to be unambiguous: a finished response and a dropped connection must not look the same.

sections.title: Reserve capacity before spending it
paragraphs: A Redis-backed generation guard makes admission and cost tracking explicit. A reservation represents the expected spend before the provider call starts. Completion settles the reservation against actual usage, and a request that has not incurred spend releases its hold.

The reasoning is about concurrency. If several generations start at once and cost is only recorded afterwards, the total exposure is unknown until they finish. Reserving first means each request claims part of a budget before it can spend, so the amount that can be in flight at once is bounded. The purpose is to control concurrent generation spend.

The guard uses user-scoped locks and ownership tokens. Cleanup must not delete a lock that expired and was then acquired by another request, so interruption handling respects who owns the work. As background, this is a common pattern with Redis locks: a token proves that the party releasing a lock is the one that acquired it.
These mechanisms bound concurrent generation exposure. They are not a claim about reduced model bills, which still depend on pricing, token usage and real demand.

What I would be careful about is the estimate. A reservation is an expected amount, and the real usage may differ. The settle step exists to reconcile the two, which is why the diagram ends every path in settle or release. I have not measured how close the estimate is to actual usage, so I treat that comparison as a first-order metric rather than a property I can assert.

stateDiagram-v2

diagrams.caption: Reservation lifecycle. The sources state reserve, settle against actual usage, and release when no spend was incurred; which interruption cases settle and which release is a design question about the mechanism, not a measured behavior.

sections.title: Treat cancellation as part of the lifecycle
paragraphs: A user leaving a screen is a normal event. I worked on cancellation cleanup so interrupted generation does not leave resources reserved indefinitely.

The useful question is what had already happened when the request stopped: was a provider call started, did it incur usage, was a result persisted, and which cleanup is still safe? Reasoning about those transitions keeps cost tracking and user-visible state aligned.

A request that stops before the provider call has nothing to settle, so releasing the hold is the natural outcome. A request that stops after text has been generated may already have incurred usage, so the accounting should reflect that rather than pretend nothing happened. The diagram at the top of the article shows this as release or settle by usage, and it is the part of the design most sensitive to implementation detail.

Cancellation is easy to under-test because it does not fail loudly. If cleanup is skipped, nothing crashes; a hold simply stays in place and a later request is affected. For that reason I think of cancellation as a path that deserves the same design attention as completion, with the same question asked at each stage: what state do we own, and what is safe to release.

table.caption: Interruption points and the question each one asks. This is a reasoning aid, not a log of observed behavior.
rows: During generation, before text is sent
Settle by usage, or release if none
Clean up and keep accounting aligned

sections.title: Keep entitlement and identity consistent
paragraphs: Subscription webhooks and account changes can arrive outside the active app session. I worked on webhook reconciliation and account-merge consistency, so access follows durable account state instead of whatever a client screen last showed.

As background, a webhook is a message a billing service sends to your backend when something changes, and it may be delivered more than once or out of order. Reconciling means the backend applies an event in a way that tolerates repeats and reordering, so the same input leads to the same stored state. Account merges add a second concern: when two identities become one, the entitlement and records that belong to the account must stay attached to the surviving identity.

Duplicate or reordered events, sign-in transitions and interrupted updates all need explicit handling. Local checks cover the implementation, but purchase, restore, refund and identity-provider flows still need validation against the real services and devices.

The design principle is that the client is a view of the account, not the authority on it. A screen can show stale access if a purchase finished moments ago or a restore is in progress, so the backend decision uses durable state. This also means the client can be simple: it asks what access the account has instead of reasoning about subscription events itself.

flowchart TD

    C -- "yes" --> D["Ignore duplicate"]
    C -- "no" --> E["Reconcile with stored state"]
    E --> F["Update durable entitlement"]
    F --> G["Client reads current access"]
diagrams.caption: Generic webhook reconciliation flow: identify the account, tolerate duplicates, update durable state, and let the client read it. This is an abstraction of the reconciliation work, not the real handler.

sections.title: Design privacy into storage and observability
paragraphs: Private text should not become routine diagnostic output. The backend encrypts private text and uses privacy-conscious telemetry that keeps operational events separate from the substance of a reflection.

The trade-off is that debugging is less convenient when raw content is unavailable. The answer is to define useful event types, failure categories and correlation identifiers early, not to log personal entries by default. An event such as a generation that ended early, with a category and an identifier, is enough to find the request without storing what the person wrote.

The same principle applies to generation input. Private text is needed to produce a response, but needing it in one place does not justify copying it into every log, metric or error report. Keeping the path that handles the text separate from the path that reports on the system limits where personal writing can end up. I have not audited the product against a formal privacy standard, and I make no compliance claim.

diagrams.chart:
flowchart TD
    P["Private reflection text"] --> S["Encrypted storage"]
    P --> G["Generation request"]
    G --> O["Operational events"]
    O --> T["Telemetry: event type, category, id"]
    P -. "kept out" .-> T
diagrams.caption: Data boundary: private text goes to encrypted storage and the generation path, while telemetry carries only operational information. The exact fields in telemetry are not specified in the sources.

sections.title: What has been verified and what has not
paragraphs: PRISM covers mobile interaction, streaming APIs, persistent data, generation guards and subscription handling end to end. I prepared release checks and local validation. That is the extent of what I claim: local checks of the implementation, not results from a launched product.

Not yet verified are the real purchase, restore, refund and identity-provider flows on real devices, the full product in its deployment context, and any figure about cost, completion or quality. I include no launch date, pricing, revenue or user count because none is established.

The distinction matters for a product of this kind. A reflection app handles personal writing, and a payment flow handles money, so the cases that matter most are the ones that are hardest to exercise locally: a restore on a second device, a refund arriving after access was granted, a merge of two sign-in methods. Those are the checks I would want complete before describing the system as ready.

sections.title: What to measure next
paragraphs: Before publishing numbers I would collect completion and interruption rates, response quality feedback, cost per completed interaction, and results from real purchase and restore tests. Source code alone cannot establish those.

Each metric maps to a mechanism above. Interruption rate tests whether cancellation cleanup matters in practice, cost per completed interaction tests the reservation estimate against actual usage, and purchase and restore results test webhook reconciliation. Until then, the accurate summary is that the mechanisms are built and in internal QA.

takeaways: Streaming creates states a plain request does not have: admitted, generating, partial, interrupted. Design the cleanup path for each.
Reserve expected spend before the provider call and settle or release afterwards, so concurrent exposure is bounded.
Ownership tokens stop cleanup from removing a lock that now belongs to another request.
Entitlement should follow durable account state, with webhook handling that tolerates duplicate and reordered events.
Keep private text out of telemetry by defining useful event types and identifiers up front. PRISM is in internal QA and no outcome claims are made.
